artworks.title: Yokosuka
artworks.description: A blurred, raw street scene from the port and base town of Yokosuka, made in the are-bure-boke manner of the Provoke years.

name: Diane Arbus
tagline: A photograph is a secret about a secret
bio: Diane Arbus left fashion photography to make square, flash-lit portraits of New Yorkers at the margins and the supposed center alike — twins, giants, nudists, couples, children — meeting each subject with an unsettling directness. Her work was a centerpiece of the landmark 1967 "New Documents" exhibition at MoMA, and a posthumous 1972 retrospective made her one of the most influential and debated photographers of the century. She died by suicide in 1971, leaving images that remain provocations about looking and difference.

artworks.title: Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey
artworks.description: Two seven-year-old sisters in matching dresses stand side by side, one faintly smiling, one faintly not — sameness made eerie.

artworks.title: Child with a Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park, N.Y.C.
artworks.description: A thin boy clutches a toy grenade, face clenched in a sudden grimace — childhood caught at a fault line of tension.

artworks.title: A Young Man in Curlers at Home on West 20th Street, N.Y.C.
artworks.description: A young man sits in hair curlers, cigarette poised, returning the camera's gaze with cool composure — Arbus's frank, level attention to identity.

name: Garry Winogrand
tagline: I photograph to see what things look like photographed
bio: Garry Winogrand prowled the streets of New York and later Los Angeles with a wide-angle Leica, shooting with restless intensity and a tilted horizon that made the city feel charged and off-balance. He sought, in his own words, to see what the world looked like photographed, and produced books including "The Animals" (1969), "Women Are Beautiful" (1975) and "Public Relations" (1977). When he died he left roughly a third of a million unedited exposures, the sheer volume itself a portrait of postwar American restlessness.

artworks.title: World's Fair, New York City
artworks.description: A long bench crowded with young people, each turned a different way — a frieze of glances and gestures caught in a single sweeping frame.
artworks.credit: © The Estate of Garry Winogrand / Fraenkel Gallery

artworks.title: Los Angeles, California
artworks.description: Pedestrians cross a sun-flattened intersection, a woman in a wheelchair among them — the casual collisions of the American street.
artworks.credit: © The Estate of Garry Winogrand / Fraenkel Gallery

artworks.title: New York
artworks.description: A laughing woman strides through the crowd, hair and motion blurring — Winogrand's electric, unguarded view of city energy.
artworks.credit: © The Estate of Garry Winogrand / Fraenkel Gallery

name: Helen Levitt
tagline: The poetry of the New York sidewalk
bio: Helen Levitt spent decades photographing the streets of working-class New York — especially the improvised theater of children at play, the chalk drawings they left on pavements, and the gestures of daily life in Harlem and the Lower East Side. Encouraged by Walker Evans and championed early by Edward Steichen, who gave her a 1943 MoMA show, she worked with a discreet right-angle viewfinder to catch unposed moments. She was also a pioneer of color street photography in the 1950s and '70s, though much of that early work was lost to a burglary.

artworks.title: New York
artworks.description: Children clamber over a stoop and sidewalk in masks and mid-game — the unscripted choreography of street play Levitt made her subject.

name: Joel Meyerowitz
tagline: A pioneer of color on the New York street
bio: Joel Meyerowitz took up the camera in 1962 after watching Robert Frank work, and joined the restless generation of New York street photographers around Garry Winogrand and Tony Ray-Jones. While many peers held to black and white, in 1972 he committed himself almost entirely to color, helping win it acceptance as a serious medium. His books "Cape Light" (1978) and the street-rooted "Bystander: A History of Street Photography" (co-written with Colin Westerbeck, 1994) became landmarks. His work moves between crowded, quick-witted street frames and luminous large-format studies of light.

artworks.title: Paris, France
artworks.description: A man lies fallen at a busy intersection while passers-by glance but step over him — Meyerowitz catching the street's casual indifference.

artworks.title: New York City
artworks.description: Early black-and-white New York work from the year Meyerowitz began photographing, dense with overlapping gestures and glances.

artworks.title: New York City
artworks.description: Figures in tan coats walk away into a billow of street steam, an early color frame that turned everyday Manhattan into something cinematic.

name: Lee Friedlander
tagline: The American social landscape
bio: Lee Friedlander turned the cluttered American street — signs, store windows, fences, traffic, and his own shadow and reflection — into a dense, witty visual landscape. Emerging in the 1960s alongside Winogrand and Arbus, he was central to the 1967 "New Documents" show at MoMA that announced a new, personal documentary style. His monographs, including "Self Portrait" (1970) and "The American Monument" (1976), explore how the photographer is inescapably present in, and reflected by, the world he records.

artworks.title: New York City
artworks.description: The photographer's own shadow falls across a woman's back on the sidewalk — the watcher pressed inescapably into the scene.

artworks.title: Self Portrait, New Orleans
artworks.description: Friedlander's reflection hovers in a mirror amid the bric-a-brac of a room — identity dispersed through glass and clutter.

name: Lisette Model
tagline: Close, candid and unsparing
bio: Lisette Model was born in Vienna, trained in music, and turned to photography in the 1930s, making her first major series along the seafront promenade in Nice. Emigrating to New York in 1938, she photographed the city's nightclub patrons, Bowery characters and Coney Island bathers with a tight, frontal, unsentimental closeness that helped define modern American street photography. Her pictures appeared in Harper's Bazaar and were collected by MoMA. As a teacher at the New School she profoundly shaped a generation, most famously her student Diane Arbus.

artworks.title: Coney Island Bather, New York
artworks.description: A heavyset woman reclines on the sand and grins straight at the camera — Model's most iconic image, an everyday goddess of the beach.

artworks.title: Promenade des Anglais, Nice
artworks.description: A seated woman on the Nice seafront, photographed close and from below in the biting style of Model's first major series.

artworks.title: Reflections, New York
artworks.description: Mannequins and passers-by merge in a shop-window reflection on a Manhattan street, a study of the city's layered surfaces.

name: Vivian Maier
tagline: The nanny who photographed in secret
bio: Vivian Maier worked as a nanny in Chicago and New York while quietly making one of the great bodies of 20th-century street photography — over 100,000 negatives almost none of which she ever printed or showed. Discovered by chance at a storage-locker auction shortly before her death, her sharp, compassionate, often witty pictures of city life, and her many mirrored self-portraits, turned an unknown into a posthumous icon.

artworks.title: Self-Portrait
artworks.description: Maier frames herself in a shop mirror, Rolleiflex at her waist — the watcher who insisted on appearing in her own record.

artworks.title: New York
artworks.description: A street encounter caught at close range — the unguarded faces of the city she observed for decades.

artworks.title: Chicago
artworks.description: Gesture, shadow and reflection arranged with an instinctive eye, in pictures she kept entirely to herself.

name: Mario Giacomelli
tagline: Stark black and white from the Italian Marches
bio: Mario Giacomelli was a self-taught photographer and printer from Senigallia on Italy's Adriatic coast, who ran a small printing workshop while making some of the most graphically intense photography of the postwar period. He worked in extreme high-contrast black and white, often photographing the people and landscapes of his own region. His series of young seminarians playing in the snow, "Io non ho mani che mi accarezzino il volto" (1961–63), and his study of the hill town of Scanno (1957–59) brought him international recognition, including inclusion in MoMA's collection.

artworks.title: Io non ho mani che mi accarezzino il volto
artworks.description: Young priests in black cassocks whirl and play in the snow, reduced to dark shapes on blinding white — Giacomelli's most famous image.

artworks.title: Scanno
artworks.description: A small boy stands amid black-clad figures in the streets of the Abruzzi hill town of Scanno, a study in stark tonal contrast.

artworks.title: Verrà la morte e avrà i tuoi occhi
artworks.description: An unflinching close portrait from Giacomelli's series on the elderly in a hospice, named for a poem by Cesare Pavese.
artworks.series: Verrà la morte e avrà i tuoi occhi

name: Robert Doisneau
tagline: The warm humanist of the Paris street
bio: Robert Doisneau was, with Henri Cartier-Bresson and Willy Ronis, a leading figure of French humanist photography, devoting his life to the streets and suburbs of Paris and its working people. He worked as an advertising and industrial photographer before turning to the candid, often tender and witty street scenes for which he is loved. His most famous picture, "Le Baiser de l'hôtel de ville" (1950), made for Life magazine, became one of the most reproduced photographs of the century. He photographed Paris for some sixty years.

artworks.title: Le Baiser de l'hôtel de ville
artworks.description: A young couple kiss while walking past a café terrace near Paris City Hall — the picture that came to symbolize romantic Paris.

artworks.title: L'information scolaire
artworks.description: A puzzled schoolboy at his desk while a neighbor sneaks a glance at his slate — Doisneau's gentle humor in a Paris classroom.

artworks.title: Les frères, rue du Docteur Lecène, Paris
artworks.description: Two small boys run together down a Paris street, an early image of the working-class childhood Doisneau returned to throughout his life.

name: Robert Frank
tagline: The outsider who saw America
bio: Robert Frank emigrated from Switzerland and, on a Guggenheim fellowship, drove tens of thousands of miles across the United States in 1955 and 1956 to make the pictures that became "The Americans". Published in France in 1958 and in the U.S. in 1959 with an introduction by Jack Kerouac, the book's grainy, tilted, melancholy view of postwar America was first attacked and then revered, reshaping the language of documentary and street photography. He later turned largely to film, including the 1959 Beat film "Pull My Daisy".

artworks.title: Trolley—New Orleans
artworks.description: Passengers framed in the windows of a segregated streetcar, white riders forward and Black riders behind — a single frame holding the racial divide of 1950s America.
artworks.credit: © Robert Frank / Estate of Robert Frank

artworks.title: Parade—Hoboken, New Jersey
artworks.description: Two figures watch a parade from windows, one half-hidden by a draped flag — patriotism made strange and faintly ominous.
artworks.credit: © Robert Frank / Estate of Robert Frank

artworks.title: Elevator—Miami Beach
artworks.description: A blurred crowd surrounds a young elevator operator caught in a moment of private reverie — solitude inside the machinery of leisure.
artworks.credit: © Robert Frank / Estate of Robert Frank

name: Shomei Tomatsu
tagline: Postwar Japan under the American shadow
bio: Shomei Tomatsu was among the most influential Japanese photographers of the postwar era, taking as his great subject the collision between traditional Japan, the trauma of the atomic bombings and the pervasive American military presence. His series "Chewing Gum and Chocolate" (begun 1959) documented life around US bases, while his Nagasaki work of 1960–61 produced searing images of bomb survivors and relics. A co-founder of the agency Vivo, he helped lay the ground for the Provoke generation and photographers like Daido Moriyama.

artworks.title: Melted Bottle, Nagasaki
artworks.description: A glass bottle warped and fused by the heat of the atomic blast, photographed as a relic that resembles charred flesh.

artworks.title: Wristwatch Stopped at 11:02, August 9, 1945, Nagasaki
artworks.description: A corroded wristwatch frozen at the moment of the bombing, recovered from the ruins of Nagasaki.

name: Tony Ray-Jones
tagline: The gentle eccentricity of English leisure
bio: Tony Ray-Jones studied in the United States, where he absorbed the lessons of New York street photographers including Garry Winogrand and Joel Meyerowitz, before returning to England in the mid-1960s. There he set out to record the English at leisure — at seaside resorts, carnivals, dog shows and festivals — with a sardonic, affectionate eye for national eccentricity. He died of leukemia at thirty, and his work was gathered posthumously in the book "A Day Off: An English Journal" (1974). He became a decisive influence on later British photographers such as Martin Parr.

artworks.title: Beachy Head Tripper Boat
artworks.description: Day-trippers crowd a pleasure boat off the Sussex coast, their faces and poses turned into a wry catalogue of Englishness.
artworks.credit: © Tony Ray-Jones / National Science and Media Museum

artworks.title: Glyndebourne
artworks.description: Opera-goers picnic on the lawns at Glyndebourne, formal dress set against the open grass in Ray-Jones's gently absurd view of society ritual.
artworks.credit: © Tony Ray-Jones / National Science and Media Museum

artworks.title: Ramsgate
artworks.description: Holidaymakers at the seaside resort of Ramsgate, caught in the layered, faintly surreal compositions that define his English journal.
artworks.credit: © Tony Ray-Jones / National Science and Media Museum

name: William Klein
tagline: The street as a contact sheet of the world
bio: William Klein attacked street photography from the inside, shooting his native New York with a wide-angle lens, blur, grain and high contrast that broke every rule of "good" technique. His 1956 book "Life Is Good and Good for You in New York" — confrontational, kinetic, and laid out like a tabloid — won the Prix Nadar and influenced a generation, even as American publishers initially rejected it. He went on to make caustic fashion photographs and satirical films, treating the camera as a tool to provoke rather than to merely record.

artworks.title: Gun 1, New York
artworks.description: A boy thrusts a toy pistol at the lens, face contorted in mock fury — Klein's combustible, in-your-face vision of the city.
artworks.series: Life Is Good and Good for You in New York

artworks.title: Dance in Brooklyn, New York
artworks.description: Couples blur across a crowded dance floor, motion smeared into the grain — energy caught rather than frozen.
artworks.series: Life Is Good and Good for You in New York

artworks.title: Candy Store, Amsterdam Avenue, New York
artworks.description: Children swarm a storefront jammed with signs and sweets — the visual overload of the New York street pushed to the edge.
artworks.series: Life Is Good and Good for You in New York

name: Willy Ronis
tagline: Tenderness in the working-class quarters of Paris
bio: Willy Ronis was one of the great French humanist photographers, alongside Robert Doisneau and Henri Cartier-Bresson, drawn above all to the working-class neighborhoods of Paris such as Belleville and Ménilmontant. The son of a portrait photographer, he photographed lovers, factory workers, children and everyday Parisian life with warmth and a strong sense of composition. His images "Le Nu provençal" (1949) and "Les Amoureux de la Bastille" (1957) are among the best-loved photographs of the century. He continued working into his nineties.

artworks.title: Le Nu provençal
artworks.description: His wife washes at a basin in their rustic Provence home, light pouring through a shuttered window — a spontaneous, tender nude.
artworks.credit: © Willy Ronis / Ministère de la Culture

artworks.title: Les Amoureux de la Bastille
artworks.description: A young couple lean together above the rooftops of Paris, the city spread out behind them — one of Ronis's most romantic images.
artworks.credit: © Willy Ronis / Ministère de la Culture

artworks.title: Le Petit Parisien
artworks.description: A boy runs down a street clutching a baguette nearly as big as himself, a quintessential image of Parisian childhood.
artworks.credit: © Willy Ronis / Ministère de la Culture

name: Alex Webb
tagline: Intense colour, layered light and shadow
bio: Alex Webb began photographing in black and white but turned decisively to colour in 1978, after work in the Caribbean and Mexico convinced him that the heat and light of those places demanded it. His pictures are densely layered, built from intense colour, deep shadow and multiple planes of action compressed into a single complex frame. A Magnum member since the late 1970s, he has worked across the U.S.-Mexico border, Haiti and the tropics, gathering this work in books such as "Hot Light/Half-Made Worlds". He is regarded as a key figure in American colour photography.

artworks.title: Boquillas, Mexico
artworks.description: A figure leaping from a wall, seemingly hand-in-hand with his own shadow, in one of Webb's best-known border photographs.

artworks.title: La Gonâve, Haiti
artworks.description: A crowd gathered on the shore, the scene layered with intense Caribbean light and colour characteristic of Webb's work.

artworks.title: Tehuantepec, Mexico
artworks.description: A complex street tableau from Webb's Mexican work, compressing several actions into a single saturated frame.

name: William Eggleston
tagline: The democratic camera, in colour
bio: William Eggleston did more than anyone to win colour photography a place on the museum wall. His 1976 show at New York's MoMA — saturated dye-transfer prints of the everyday American South, tricycles, diner ceilings, gas stations — was attacked and then canonised. His "democratic camera" treats every subject as equally worthy of attention, finding strangeness and beauty in the overlooked vernacular.

artworks.title: The Red Ceiling (Greenwood, Mississippi)
artworks.description: A blood-red ceiling and bare bulb in lurid dye-transfer — perhaps the most famous colour photograph ever made.

artworks.title: Untitled (Tricycle)
artworks.description: A child's tricycle shot from below, monumental against suburban houses — the ordinary made heroic.

artworks.title: Memphis
artworks.description: Everyday Southern interiors and signs rendered in rich, deliberate colour — the democratic eye at work.

name: Ernst Haas
tagline: An early evangelist of expressive colour
bio: Born in Vienna, Ernst Haas became one of the earliest photographers to embrace colour as a serious creative medium, at a time when it was dismissed as commercial. His 1953 "Magic Images of a City" essay in Life magazine — a 24-page colour portrait of New York — was a landmark for the magazine and the form. Using slow shutter speeds to dissolve movement into streaks of colour, Haas pursued an emotional, almost abstract lyricism quite distinct from the deadpan New Color school that followed.

artworks.title: Route 66, Albuquerque, New Mexico
artworks.description: Neon, asphalt and the open American road rendered in Haas's rich, saturated colour.

artworks.title: Reflections, New York
artworks.description: Glass facades mirroring the city into one another, from Haas's pioneering colour vision of New York.

artworks.title: Rodeo, New York
artworks.description: A blur of motion and colour as Haas uses a slow shutter to turn action into painterly abstraction.

name: Eve Sonneman
tagline: Colour diptychs and the slippage of time
bio: Eve Sonneman built her work around the photographic diptych, pairing two frames of the same scene moments apart to register the slippage of time and attention. Beginning with black-and-white pairs during her studies at the University of New Mexico in the late 1960s, she moved into colour diptychs through the 1970s. Her professional breakthrough came with the "Young Photographers" show at MoMA in 1971, and her work appeared in the era-defining exhibition "Mirrors and Windows: American Photography since 1960". Her quietly conceptual use of colour and sequence made her a distinctive voice in the new colour photography.

artworks.title: Coney Island, New York
artworks.description: A paired beach and street scene typical of Sonneman's diptychs, two near-identical moments revealing the passage of time.

artworks.title: Greece
artworks.description: A colour diptych made abroad, the doubled frame turning an ordinary scene into a study of perception and sequence.

artworks.title: New York
artworks.description: An urban pairing from the period of "Mirrors and Windows", Sonneman's quietly conceptual approach to colour and time.

name: Fred Herzog
tagline: Kodachrome streets of postwar Vancouver
bio: Born in Germany and settled in Vancouver, Fred Herzog spent decades photographing the city's working-class streets, neon signs, shop windows and people in colour from the 1950s onward. He worked almost entirely on Kodachrome slide film at a time when fine-art photography meant black and white, and the difficulty of printing those slides kept his work obscure for years. Critical recognition came only late in life, with a major 2007 retrospective at the Vancouver Art Gallery. His richly saturated images now read as a pioneering body of colour street photography.

artworks.title: Bogner's Grocery
artworks.description: A Vancouver storefront in warm Kodachrome colour; the image was later issued as a Canada Post stamp celebrating Canadian photography.

artworks.title: Man with Bandage
artworks.description: A candid street portrait typical of Herzog's eye for ordinary city life rendered in vivid colour.

artworks.title: Red Stockings
artworks.description: A shop window display whose saturated reds show Herzog's early, unfashionable embrace of colour film.

name: Harry Gruyaert
tagline: European colour from Morocco to Belgium
bio: Harry Gruyaert was among the first European photographers to commit entirely to colour, inspired by Pop art and by a trip to Morocco in 1969. Working in a register closer to painting than to reportage, he built images from atmospheric light and bold blocks of colour across Belgium, Morocco, Egypt and the United States. He joined Magnum Photos in 1982, an unusual step for a colourist within an agency rooted in black-and-white documentary tradition. His books, including "Morocco" and "Rivages", established him as a leading European voice in colour photography.

artworks.title: Morocco
artworks.description: A sun-drenched Moroccan scene from the country that first convinced Gruyaert colour was his medium, all warm light and saturated walls.

artworks.title: Belgium
artworks.description: An overcast, muted view of Gruyaert's native Belgium, its subdued northern light contrasting with his radiant Mediterranean work.

artworks.title: Las Vegas, USA
artworks.description: An American scene from the early 1980s, the artificial colour and light of the West filtered through Gruyaert's painterly eye.

name: Jan Groover
tagline: Kitchen still lifes and formal colour
bio: Trained as a painter, Jan Groover brought a formalist's eye to colour photography, treating composition and the play of space as her true subjects. After receiving an NEA grant in 1978 she bought a large-format camera and began her celebrated "Kitchen Still Lifes", transforming colanders, knives and pastry tins into luminous abstract arrangements. Using artificial light, glass and careful staging, she turned domestic clutter into studies of form, reflection and colour. A major figure in 1970s and 1980s American photography, she was given solo exhibitions at MoMA and the Whitney.

artworks.title: Untitled (Kitchen Still Life)
artworks.description: Everyday kitchen utensils arranged into a luminous, near-abstract composition of form, reflection and colour.

name: Joel Sternfeld
tagline: Ironic American prospects in large-format colour
bio: Joel Sternfeld travelled the United States between 1978 and 1983 on a Guggenheim Fellowship, working with an 8x10 view camera. The resulting book, "American Prospects" (1987), became an early monument of colour photography, balancing lush, descriptive colour with a dry, often unsettling wit. His tableaux pair the beauty of the American landscape with quiet absurdity and disaster, extending the documentary tradition of Walker Evans and Robert Frank into colour.

artworks.title: McLean, Virginia, December 1978
artworks.description: A fireman calmly selects pumpkins at a farm stand while a house burns behind him — Sternfeld's most famous, deadpan tableau.

artworks.title: Approximately 17 of 41 Sperm Whales That Beached and Subsequently Died, Florence, Oregon
artworks.description: Stranded whales on a grey Oregon beach, from "American Prospects" — landscape, catastrophe and spectacle held in cool balance.

artworks.title: Wet 'n Wild Aquatic Theme Park, Orlando, Florida
artworks.description: A drained water park rendered in saturated colour, the American leisure landscape made strange and melancholy.

name: Saul Leiter
tagline: Painterly colour on the winter street
bio: A painter who drifted into photography, Saul Leiter made colour pictures decades before the art world took colour seriously. Working a few blocks around his New York neighbourhood, he shot through steamed glass, rain, awnings and reflections, flattening the street into soft, abstract planes of muted colour — quiet, oblique and unhurried, rediscovered only late in his life.

artworks.title: Taxi
artworks.description: A red smear of taxi seen through misted glass — the city dissolved into colour and weather.

artworks.title: Snow
artworks.description: Figures muffled against falling snow, composed like a watercolour in narrow bands of tone.

artworks.title: Through Glass
artworks.description: Reflection layered over reflection — Leiter's signature flattening of the street into abstraction.

name: Luigi Ghirri
tagline: Quiet conceptual colour of the Italian everyday
bio: Luigi Ghirri was the central figure of Italian colour photography, a former surveyor who turned the camera on the ordinary landscape of his native Emilia and beyond. His self-published 1978 book "Kodachrome" gathered tightly framed images of walls, windows, postcards, advertisements and potted plants — photographs about looking and representation as much as about places. Working in modest, meticulous prints, he argued simply that "the real world is in colour". His conceptual yet tender vision made him one of Europe's most influential photographers, admired far beyond Italy.

artworks.title: Modena
artworks.description: A characteristically quiet image of Ghirri's home region, from the "Kodachrome" period that defined Italian conceptual colour photography.

artworks.title: Marina di Ravenna
artworks.description: A coastal scene rendered in subtle Kodachrome tones, ordinary Italian leisure observed with cool, conceptual attention.

artworks.title: Île Rousse
artworks.description: A tightly framed view from Ghirri's travels, a meditation on landscape, edge and the act of looking.

name: Martin Parr
tagline: Saturated, satirical British colour
bio: Martin Parr brought a sharp, satirical eye to British social life, using saturated colour and daylight flash to scrutinise consumerism, leisure and class. His breakthrough series "The Last Resort", made at the run-down seaside resort of New Brighton between 1983 and 1985, drew both acclaim and controversy when it appeared in 1986. Influenced by American colour photographers such as William Eggleston, Parr turned the everyday rituals of holidaymakers and shoppers into pointed social documents. A Magnum member, he has since become one of the most recognisable documentary photographers working in colour.

artworks.title: New Brighton, England (from The Last Resort)
artworks.description: A crowded, litter-strewn seaside scene from "The Last Resort", Parr's caustic, brightly coloured portrait of a declining English resort.

artworks.title: The Last Resort, New Brighton
artworks.description: An early frame from the series that brought Parr to public attention and helped define his saturated documentary style.

name: Mitch Epstein
tagline: American leisure in early fine-art colour
bio: Mitch Epstein helped pioneer fine-art colour photography in the 1970s alongside William Eggleston, Joel Meyerowitz and Stephen Shore. Arriving in New York in 1973 to study under Garry Winogrand at Cooper Union, he soon abandoned black and white for the lush palette of colour film, then still taboo in the art world. His long project "Recreation" (1973–1988) cast a wry, observant eye on how Americans spent their leisure time. He later turned to large-format work in India and to the landscape of American energy, but his early colour pictures remain foundational.

artworks.title: Cocoa Beach, Florida
artworks.description: A study of American leisure from "Recreation", everyday vacationers observed with subtle, saturated colour.

artworks.title: Untitled, New York
artworks.description: An early colour frame made soon after Epstein took up the medium under Garry Winogrand's influence.

artworks.title: Untitled, India
artworks.description: A scene from Epstein's extended work in India, the daily life and colour of the subcontinent seen by a colour pioneer abroad.

name: Nan Goldin
tagline: Snapshot intimacy in flash-lit colour
bio: Nan Goldin made the snapshot a vehicle for raw emotional truth, photographing her circle of friends, lovers and chosen family with an unflinching closeness. Built between 1973 and 1986, "The Ballad of Sexual Dependency" began as a slide show set to music and became a landmark book in 1986, charting love, addiction, desire and loss. Her on-camera flash and saturated Cibachrome prints gave colour photography a new emotional register, far from the cool detachment of her contemporaries. The work transformed how intimacy and autobiography could be addressed in the medium.

artworks.title: Nan and Brian in Bed, New York City
artworks.description: A charged domestic moment from "The Ballad of Sexual Dependency", the artist and her lover caught in flash-lit colour.

artworks.title: Twisting at My Birthday Party, New York City
artworks.description: Friends dancing at a party, the snapshot intimacy and warm colour that define Goldin's chronicle of her chosen family.

artworks.title: C.Z. and Max on the Beach, Truro, Massachusetts
artworks.description: An early image from the "Ballad", tender and direct, made among the friends who populate Goldin's lifelong project.

name: Stephen Shore
tagline: The American road in deadpan colour
bio: Stephen Shore helped legitimise colour as serious art with cross-country road trips made between 1973 and 1981. Trading a 35mm camera for large-format 4x5 and then 8x10 view cameras, he photographed motels, parking lots, intersections and diner meals with cool, frontal precision. Collected as "Uncommon Places", the pictures turned the banal American vernacular into rigorously composed, richly detailed documents. His earlier "American Surfaces" had already pushed the snapshot toward fine art.

artworks.title: U.S. 93, Kingman, Arizona
artworks.description: A wide desert highway under open sky, from "Uncommon Places" — the American road rendered with view-camera clarity.

artworks.title: Beverly Boulevard and La Brea Avenue, Los Angeles, California
artworks.description: A frontal study of an ordinary Los Angeles intersection, every sign and surface given equal, deadpan attention.

artworks.title: Merced River, Yosemite National Park, California
artworks.description: A luminous river landscape that brings Shore's precise colour and structure to the grand American scenic tradition.

name: William Christenberry
tagline: The slow weathering of the rural South
bio: William Christenberry returned almost every year for four decades to Hale County, Alabama, the territory of his childhood and of Walker Evans's Depression-era work. Beginning in the 1960s he photographed its weathered churches, warehouses and storefronts, often re-shooting the same buildings to record their slow decline. Working at first with a simple Brownie camera, his tender, frontal colour images form a prolonged meditation on place, memory and the passage of time.

artworks.title: Green Warehouse, Newbern, Alabama
artworks.description: A warped green tin warehouse standing alone — one of Christenberry's most iconic and repeatedly revisited subjects.

artworks.title: Church, Sprott, Alabama
artworks.description: A small white frame church set against the Alabama landscape, photographed with quiet, frontal devotion.

artworks.title: Coleman's Cafe, Greensboro, Alabama
artworks.description: A modest rural cafe, part of Christenberry's decades-long record of vernacular Southern architecture and its weathering.

name: Andreas Gursky
tagline: The monumental scale of globalized life
bio: Andreas Gursky makes vast, often digitally composited photographs that survey the spaces of contemporary capitalism — stock exchanges, supermarkets, factories, rivers and crowds — from a high, detached vantage. A student of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Düsseldorf Academy, he inherited their frontal, systematic eye and enlarged it to mural scale and saturated color. His pictures flatten teeming detail into near-abstract pattern, turning the man-altered world into images of overwhelming, almost sublime order.

artworks.title: Paris, Montparnasse
artworks.description: The vast facade of a Montparnasse housing block rendered as an endless grid of identical apartments.

artworks.title: 99 Cent II Diptychon
artworks.description: The interior of a discount store, its shelves an explosive grid of repeating color and consumer abundance.

name: Bernd & Hilla Becher
tagline: Typologies of anonymous industry
bio: Bernd and Hilla Becher spent five decades photographing the vanishing industrial architecture of Europe and North America — water towers, blast furnaces, winding towers and grain elevators — in a uniform, frontal, even light. They arranged these black-and-white pictures into grids they called "typologies," inviting comparison of function and form and elevating utilitarian structures into what they termed "anonymous sculptures." Included in the 1975 "New Topographics" show, their detached, systematic method shaped the Düsseldorf School they taught, influencing Gursky, Struth and Höfer.

artworks.title: Water Towers
artworks.description: A grid of frontal portraits of water towers — the typological method that defined their life's work.

artworks.title: Winding Towers
artworks.description: Nine pithead winding towers assembled into variations on an ideal industrial form.

artworks.title: Blast Furnaces
artworks.description: Towering steelworks furnaces recorded under flat skies, monumental and obsolescent.

name: Candida Höfer
tagline: The grandeur of empty public space
bio: Candida Höfer photographs the interiors of libraries, museums, theatres, opera houses and palaces, almost always devoid of people. A first-generation student of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Düsseldorf Academy, she renders these civic and cultural rooms in cool color from a frontal or diagonal vantage, with even light and exacting symmetry. The absence of human figures lends her spaces an eerie grandeur, inviting contemplation of architecture and of the social order such buildings embody.

artworks.title: Biblioteca del Escorial
artworks.description: The vaulted library of El Escorial, its shelves and frescoed ceiling held in cool, symmetrical order.

artworks.title: Teatro Olimpico Vicenza
artworks.description: Palladio's Renaissance theatre photographed empty, its tiered architecture a study in human-made grandeur.

artworks.title: Musée du Louvre Paris
artworks.description: A grand gallery of the Louvre, deserted and luminous, from her project documenting the museum's rooms.

name: Edward Burtynsky
tagline: Industry's mark on the earth, at scale
bio: Edward Burtynsky makes large-format color photographs of landscapes transformed by industry — mines, quarries, tailings ponds, oil fields and recycling yards — often shot from elevated or aerial vantages. His sweeping compositions render extraction and waste with an uneasy, formal beauty that draws viewers into images of environmental damage. Gathered in projects such as Manufactured Landscapes and Oil, his work carries the man-altered landscape to a planetary scale, documenting the cost of modern consumption.

artworks.title: Nickel Tailings #34, Sudbury, Ontario
artworks.description: A river of bright orange nickel tailings snaking down a blackened hillside, beauty drawn from toxicity.

artworks.title: Oxford Tire Pile #1, Westley, California
artworks.description: An immense landscape of discarded tires, the scale of waste rendered almost geological.

artworks.title: Highland Valley #1, Teck Cominco Open Pit Copper Mine, British Columbia
artworks.description: An open-pit copper mine carved into terraces, the earth reshaped on an overwhelming industrial scale.

name: Frank Gohlke
tagline: Grain elevators and the wounded land
bio: Frank Gohlke photographs the American landscape where human structure and natural force meet — the grain elevators of the central plains, the wreckage of a Texas tornado, and the slow regeneration of Mount St. Helens after its 1980 eruption. One of the photographers in the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, he combines documentary clarity with a contemplative, sequential eye, often returning to the same site over years to record change. His work treats the altered land less as indictment than as a subject for patient, humane attention.

artworks.title: Grain Elevator, Happy, Texas
artworks.description: A prairie grain elevator standing like a cathedral over the flat plains — the 'anonymous sculpture' of agriculture.

artworks.title: Aerial View, Mount St. Helens
artworks.description: Blown-down forests after the eruption, an entire landscape rearranged by geological violence.

artworks.title: Aftermath: The Wichita Falls, Texas, Tornado
artworks.description: The debris of his hometown after the 1979 tornado, human order undone in an instant.

name: Henry Wessel Jr.
tagline: Wry light in the American West
bio: Henry Wessel Jr. brought a street photographer's intuition to the New Topographics, making spare, wry black-and-white pictures of vernacular scenes in the American West. Drawn to the hard, clear light of California, he moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1971 and photographed bungalows, palm trees, parking lots and roadside signs with deadpan attention. One of the ten photographers in the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, he found quiet irony and formal pleasure in the most commonplace corners of the social landscape.

artworks.title: Walapai, Arizona
artworks.description: A lone roadside scene in the desert Southwest, ordinary structure isolated in raking Western light.

artworks.title: Los Angeles, California
artworks.description: Telephone poles, bungalow and bright sky, the commonplace social landscape rendered with spare clarity.

name: Joe Deal
tagline: The high, flat view of the suburb
bio: Joe Deal photographed the American West being parceled into subdivisions, favoring an elevated, horizon-less vantage that pressed the land flat against the picture plane. One of the photographers in the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, he used a square format and an even tonal range to record housing tracts, fault lines and graded hillsides without drama or comment. The result is a cool, almost cartographic study of how people reshape the ground beneath them.

artworks.title: Untitled View (Albuquerque)
artworks.description: An elevated, edge-to-edge view of desert subdivision near Albuquerque — the signature high, flat New Topographics gaze.

artworks.title: Backyard, Diamond Bar, California
artworks.description: From The Fault Zone — suburban yards built atop the seismic landscape of Southern California.

artworks.title: Colton, California
artworks.description: Graded earth and new houses pressed into a flat, dispassionate frame.

name: John Schott
tagline: The roadside vernacular of Route 66
bio: In the summer of 1973 John Schott drove Route 66 with an 8x10-inch Deardorff view camera, photographing the aging motels and roadside structures of the American highway. The resulting Route 66 Motels series presents this commercial vernacular with deadpan frontality, the road and its buildings treated as a defining feature of the landscape. Selected for the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition at George Eastman House, his work fixed the ordinary architecture of travel within the movement's detached descriptive gaze.

artworks.title: Untitled, from Route 66 Motels
artworks.description: A vintage roadside motel along Route 66, recorded frontally in the flat light of the desert highway.

artworks.title: Untitled, from Route 66 Motels
artworks.description: A motel office with pay telephone and signage, the commercial vernacular of the postwar road.

artworks.title: Untitled, from Route 66 Motels
artworks.description: Cabins and parked cars under a wide sky, the highway landscape as banal, deadpan document.

name: Lewis Baltz
tagline: The industrial park as minimal sculpture
bio: Lewis Baltz photographed the bland, anonymous edges of postwar American development — tract houses, warehouses and the blank stucco walls of new industrial parks — with the rigour of a minimalist sculptor. A central figure of the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, he treated the man-made landscape as flat, gridded fact, draining it of romance until the banal surface itself became the subject. His cool, frontal black-and-white prints turned the periphery of the boom economy into severe, formally exacting art.

artworks.title: Tract House No. 1
artworks.description: A raw plywood wall and window from The Tract Houses, recorded with deadpan, near-abstract precision.

artworks.title: South Wall, Mazda Motors, 2121 East Main Street, Irvine
artworks.description: From The New Industrial Parks near Irvine, California — a blank corporate facade as minimal geometry.

artworks.title: Park City, Interior, 41
artworks.description: From Park City, his survey of a Utah condominium development under construction, ground turned to rubble and frame.

name: Naoya Hatakeyama
tagline: Extraction, blast and the made city
bio: Naoya Hatakeyama examines the meaning of landscape in an age when all land bears the imprint of human activity. His Lime Works documented the limestone quarries and cement plants that supply the material of Japan's cities, and his Blast series froze the choreographed mining detonations that loosen the rock. Tracing the path from quarry to building to underground infrastructure, his cool, exacting photographs link the man-altered landscape directly to the urban world it makes possible.

artworks.title: Lime Works
artworks.description: A terraced limestone quarry and cement plant from Lime Works, the raw material of the modern city laid bare.

artworks.title: Blast #5416
artworks.description: A quarry detonation caught mid-explosion, rock and dust hurled into the air in a frozen instant.

artworks.title: Underground
artworks.description: A lit passage through Tokyo's subterranean waterways, the hidden infrastructure beneath the built city.

name: Nicholas Nixon
tagline: Cities and faces in 8x10 clarity
bio: Nicholas Nixon works with a large 8x10-inch view camera, prizing the tonal richness and detail of contact-scale negatives. His early cityscapes of Boston and New York were included in the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, treating the built environment with cool descriptive precision. In 1975 he also began The Brown Sisters, an annual group portrait of his wife and her three sisters that he continued for more than four decades, an extended meditation on time, aging and family.

artworks.title: View of Boston from Commercial Wharf
artworks.description: An expansive large-format cityscape of Boston, the dense urban grid rendered in fine detail — among the works shown in New Topographics.

artworks.title: View of Buildings and Trees, Boston
artworks.description: Rooftops and water towers stacked across the frame, the man-built city as topographic fact.

name: Richard Misrach
tagline: The desert as scene of human consequence
bio: Richard Misrach helped pioneer the use of large-scale color and the view camera in fine-art photography, turning his lens on the deserts of the American West. Begun in 1979, his ongoing Desert Cantos divides the work into thematic chapters that trace how military testing, fire, flood and industry have scarred the land. Combining seductive beauty with pointed environmental critique, his work extends the New Topographics' man-altered landscape into a sweeping meditation on humanity's mark on nature.

artworks.title: Desert Fire #1 (Burning Palms)
artworks.description: A line of palms ablaze in the desert night, from the Desert Cantos — beauty and destruction held together.

artworks.title: Bomb Crater and Destroyed Convoy, Bravo 20 Bombing Range, Nevada
artworks.description: A military bombing range pocked with craters and wreckage, the West turned into a target.

artworks.title: Holy Cross Cemetery and Dow Chemical Plant, Louisiana
artworks.description: From the Cancer Alley work later gathered in Petrochemical America — graves beneath an industrial skyline.

name: Robert Adams
tagline: The West, altered
bio: Robert Adams photographed the American West as it actually was in the postwar boom — tract houses, highways and clear-cut foothills under a high, flat light — rather than as romantic wilderness. A central figure of the 1975 "New Topographics" exhibition, his restrained, unspectacular pictures carry a quiet moral weight, mourning what development costs while still finding grace in the ordinary land.

artworks.title: Colorado Springs, Colorado
artworks.description: A new tract house at the edge of the plains, lit by raking sun — the suburb advancing on the West.

artworks.title: Tract House, Colorado
artworks.description: Plain construction recorded without comment — the deadpan aesthetic that defined New Topographics.

artworks.title: Mobile Homes, Jefferson County
artworks.description: The man-altered landscape: housing, road and sky in cool equilibrium.

name: Thomas Ruff
tagline: Interrogating the photographic image
bio: Thomas Ruff studied under Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Düsseldorf Academy and pushed their serial, analytic method toward a sustained inquiry into the nature of the image itself. He is best known for his monumental Porträts, deadpan passport-style portraits of friends at vast scale, and for series built from found and appropriated material such as Sterne and JPEGs. Working across photographed, archival and digital sources, he treats every image as a constructed object to be examined rather than a transparent window on reality.

artworks.title: Porträt (from Porträts)
artworks.description: A friend rendered frontally at monumental scale in the neutral manner of a passport photograph.

artworks.title: Sterne 18h 04m / -30°
artworks.description: From Sterne — a vast field of stars enlarged from European Southern Observatory archive negatives.

artworks.title: Haus Nr. 9 I (from Häuser)
artworks.description: A modernist building photographed frontally and digitally cleaned of distraction, an exemplary type.

name: Thomas Struth
tagline: Empty streets and crowded museums
bio: Thomas Struth, a member of the Düsseldorf School trained under Bernd and Hilla Becher, began in the 1970s with deserted, frontal black-and-white photographs of city streets in Düsseldorf and New York. He later turned to large color works, most famously the Museum Photographs that picture visitors before great paintings, and the dense jungle scenes of his Paradise series. Across these projects he applies the Bechers' detached, structural rigor to the built and natural world, examining how people inhabit and look at their surroundings.

artworks.title: Crosby Street, New York
artworks.description: An empty Manhattan street seen straight down its center, the city's architecture laid out as ordered fact.

artworks.title: Art Institute of Chicago II
artworks.description: From Museum Photographs — visitors gathered before masterworks, viewers and viewed held in one frame.

artworks.title: Paradise 9 (Xi Shuang Banna, Yunnan Province)
artworks.description: A wall of dense, undifferentiated jungle from the Paradise series, nature as overwhelming pattern.

name: Claude Cahun
tagline: The self as endless masquerade
bio: Born Lucy Schwob, Claude Cahun used staged self-portraiture to dissolve fixed identity decades before the idea entered the mainstream. Often working with partner Marcel Moore, Cahun adopted shifting personas — dandy, doll, weightlifter, shaven-headed androgyne — and built double exposures and mirrored compositions that interrogated gender and the subconscious. Long overlooked, this Surrealist body of work is now seen as a foundational ancestor of constructed, performative photography.

artworks.title: I am in training, don't kiss me
artworks.description: Cahun as a painted strongman with hearts on the cheeks and barbells in hand — gender restaged as theatrical costume.

artworks.title: Que me veux-tu?
artworks.description: A double self-portrait, two shaven heads conjoined — identity split and doubled through the camera.

name: Gregory Crewdson
tagline: Cinema in a single frame
bio: Gregory Crewdson builds his photographs like film productions — full crews, lighting rigs, built sets and whole closed streets — to make single, exquisitely lit frames of small-town American unease. In series such as Twilight, Beneath the Roses and Cathedral of the Pines, ordinary suburban moments are charged with mystery and dread, the constructed photograph pushed to a cinematic extreme that frames the staged surrealism of his successors.

artworks.title: Untitled (Ophelia)
artworks.description: A woman floats in a flooded living room, water rising indoors — domestic life turned uncanny and still.

artworks.title: Beneath the Roses
artworks.description: A figure stranded under twilight street lamps — cinematic light and dread in a single constructed frame.

name: Duane Michals
tagline: Photographs that tell stories
bio: Duane Michals broke with the single decisive moment by staging photographs in narrative sequences, often inscribing handwritten text directly beneath the prints. Using double exposure, ghostly blur and deadpan domestic settings, he photographed dreams, desire, death and the soul leaving the body — subjects most photographers thought impossible to picture. His sequences turned staged photography into a form of storytelling, a quietly surreal and deeply personal cinema made of stills.

artworks.title: The Spirit Leaves the Body
artworks.description: A sequence of seven frames in which a ghostly double rises from a reclining figure — the soul made visible by double exposure.

artworks.title: Chance Meeting
artworks.description: Two men pass in a narrow alley, glancing back — an intimate, ambiguous encounter staged across six frames.

artworks.title: Things Are Queer
artworks.description: A circular nine-frame riddle that pulls steadily backward through nested images — a bathroom inside a book inside a photograph.

name: Erwin Olaf
tagline: Cinematic stillness on the edge of emotion
bio: Erwin Olaf built immaculate, film-still tableaux in which carefully cast figures inhabit retro interiors charged with suppressed feeling. His celebrated trilogy Rain, Hope and Grief froze the instant just before or after an emotional rupture, lit and styled with the precision of advertising he had mastered commercially. Cool, glossy and psychologically loaded, his constructed scenes made restrained drama and ambiguity the heart of contemporary staged photography.

artworks.title: Rain, The Dancing School
artworks.description: A poised figure suspended in a Technicolor period interior — a mood held in the moment before tears.

artworks.title: Hope, Portrait #2
artworks.description: A waiting figure in a styled mid-century room, gaze averted — anticipation rendered as immaculate stillness.

artworks.title: Grief, Barbara
artworks.description: A composed woman undone by a single tear in a hushed interior — sorrow staged with cinematic precision.

artworks.description: From the staged, cinematic, often unsettling tableaux of Erwin Olaf — meticulous studio fictions of mood, period and the body.

name: Hans Bellmer
tagline: The doll endlessly recombined
bio: Hans Bellmer constructed life-size articulated dolls in 1930s Berlin, then photographed them dismembered and reassembled into impossible, eroticized anatomies. Published as Die Puppe and circulated in the Surrealist journal Minotaure, the hand-tinted images fused desire, dread and protest against the rising Nazi state. His staged photographs of the doll remain among the most disturbing and influential constructions in Surrealist photography.

artworks.title: Die Puppe (The Doll)
artworks.description: An assembled doll with exposed joints posed in a bare interior — the body rebuilt as unsettling object.

artworks.title: La Poupée
artworks.description: Hand-tinted study of the second, ball-jointed doll splayed against a stairway — anatomy multiplied and deranged.

artworks.title: Les Jeux de la Poupée
artworks.description: A doll staged amid foliage like a discovered crime — eros and violence folded into one image.

name: Jeff Wall
tagline: Cinematic tableaux on the lightbox
bio: Jeff Wall reinvented the photograph as a large-scale, meticulously constructed picture, famously presenting his images as backlit transparencies in lightboxes that echo cinema and advertising. He casts actors, scouts locations and, since the 1990s, digitally composites scenes shot over months to reconstruct fleeting events or restage works by Hokusai and Manet. His "near documentary" tableaux made elaborate staging a serious, intellectual mode of contemporary art photography.

artworks.title: Mimic
artworks.description: A restaged street moment in which a man makes a racist gesture beside an Asian passerby — an everyday slight reconstructed in detail.

artworks.title: A Sudden Gust of Wind (after Hokusai)
artworks.description: Papers scatter from startled figures in a windswept field — a Hokusai woodcut rebuilt over months and digitally composited.

artworks.title: Insomnia
artworks.description: A sleepless man sprawled on a kitchen floor under hard light — domestic unease staged as cinematic still life.

name: Joel-Peter Witkin
tagline: Beauty staged from the grotesque
bio: Joel-Peter Witkin builds dense, deliberately macabre tableaux that quote Old Master paintings while confronting death, the body and the taboo. He casts marginalized subjects, cadavers and severed body parts, then scratches, bleaches and tones his negatives so the prints arrive looking like relics dredged from another century. Equal parts reverent and transgressive, his constructed allegories pushed staged photography to its darkest and most baroque extreme.

artworks.title: Sanitarium
artworks.description: A masked woman tethered by a breathing tube to a monkey on the wall — a clinical nightmare staged with ritual care.

artworks.title: Las Meninas
artworks.description: A reworking of Velázquez's court scene with an amputee at its center — homage and shock folded into one tableau.

artworks.title: Harvest
artworks.description: An assemblage of corpses and severed limbs arranged as a still life — mortality composed like a Baroque painting.

name: Kyle Thompson
tagline: Surreal self-portraiture — solitude, smoke and abandoned places
bio:
Kyle Thompson (born January 11, 1992, in Chicago) is a self-taught fine-art photographer whose carefully staged, dreamlike self-portraits made him one of the defining surrealist photographers to emerge from the social web. He picked up a camera at nineteen, drawn to the abandoned houses and empty forests around rural Illinois, and in 2012 committed to a Flickr "365" project — one photograph a day for a year — that built an audience of tens of thousands and, after a Reddit album drew millions of views, launched his career.

His pictures are almost always of himself, shot alone with a remote timer firing bursts as he runs into frame. He builds quiet, unsettling fictions from a small vocabulary of recurring motifs — drifting smoke, billowing cloth and drapery, fire, water and submersion, faceless or fragmenting figures — rendered in warm, earthy tones inside derelict interiors and overgrown landscapes. Long shaped by anxiety, he has described the work as a kind of therapy: a way to externalise interior states as solitary, cinematic scenes.

Thompson later moved from Chicago to Portland, blending urban decay with the Pacific Northwest's forests, and developed his practice across a series of bodies of work — from the early 365 self-portraits through Plague, the flooded-town narrative Ghost Town, the more restrained Spaces Between, and the theatrical Open Stage. He has exhibited internationally (Portland, Paris, Montréal, Milan, Caserta, Rio de Janeiro), been named twice as Italian Vogue's Photo of the Day, and is represented by aA29 Project Room in Italy with his commercial archive handled by Agence VU' in Paris.

music.note: Sleepy Silver Door · Indian Bones · Dragonfly · Lady · Greensky Greenlake

artworks.title: Self-Portrait, Empty House
artworks.description: An early self-portrait from the abandoned houses around rural Illinois that drew Thompson to photography — the bare, sunlit room and lone figure that became his signature register.

artworks.title: Burning
artworks.description: Thompson famously set himself alight for several frames to make scenes of solitude feel dangerous and real — control and risk held in the same image.

artworks.title: Smoke Study
artworks.description: Drifting smoke — one of Thompson's core motifs — turns a plain interior into something charged and dreamlike.

artworks.title: 365 — Forest Figure
artworks.description: From the year-long 'one photo a day' project he posted to Flickr in 2012 — a daily discipline that built his audience and his visual language at once.

artworks.title: 365 — Cloth
artworks.description: Billowing fabric used to hide, replace or extend the body — a recurring device for turning a self-portrait into an anonymous, universal figure.

artworks.title: 365 — Submersion
artworks.description: Water and submersion recur throughout the work as images of suspension, release and the unconscious.

artworks.title: 365 — Final Frame
artworks.description: The closing image of the 365 — the project that, amplified by a Reddit album seen by millions, turned a teenager's experiment into a career.

artworks.title: Plague I
artworks.description: From the 2014 series Plague — figures masked, bound or obscured, pressing his surrealism toward something more bodily and uneasy.

artworks.title: Plague II
artworks.description: The body as site of affliction and disguise — drapery and distortion conceal identity while heightening presence.

artworks.title: Plague III
artworks.description: Warm, decaying interiors stage a private mythology of sickness and transformation.

artworks.title: Ghost Town — The Flood
artworks.description: From Ghost Town, his 2015 solo show at One Grand Gallery, Portland: a fictional flooded town drawn from childhood memory, where domestic life continues underwater.

artworks.title: Ghost Town — Submerged Room
artworks.description: Furnished interiors drowned and stilled — nostalgia and loss rendered as a place you can almost walk into.

artworks.title: Ghost Town — Floating
artworks.description: A figure suspended in the flooded town — weightless, between memory and dream.

artworks.title: Ghost Town — The House
artworks.description: The drowned house as the emotional centre of the series — a home that is both refuge and ruin.

artworks.title: Spaces Between I
artworks.description: From Spaces Between (2016–17) — a quieter, more restrained body of work concerned with thresholds, gaps and the room between one state and another.

artworks.title: Spaces Between II
artworks.description: Pared-back composition and negative space — absence doing as much work as the figure.

artworks.title: Spaces Between III
artworks.description: The interval as subject — a meditation on the unseen distances between people and within a single mind.

artworks.title: Open Stage I
artworks.description: From Open Stage (2018, aA29 Project Room, Milan; Reggia di Caserta) — the constructed scene made explicit, the world treated frankly as a set.

artworks.title: Open Stage II
artworks.description: Theatricality foregrounded — props, light and gesture acknowledge the photograph as a performance for the camera.

artworks.title: Open Stage III
artworks.description: The mature synthesis of Thompson's vocabulary — solitude, staging and warm decay composed with cinematic control.

name: Man Ray
tagline: Surrealism's photographic alchemist
bio: Born Emmanuel Radnitzky in Philadelphia, Man Ray became a central figure of Dada and Surrealism in 1920s Paris, where photography was his most inventive instrument. He treated the camera and the darkroom as tools for dream-logic, painting f-holes onto a model's back, reviving cameraless "rayographs," and rediscovering solarization. His staged, transformed images turned the human body and everyday objects into uncanny apparitions, laying the groundwork for all later constructed and surreal photography.

artworks.title: Le Violon d'Ingres
artworks.description: Kiki de Montparnasse seen from behind, two violin f-holes painted onto her back — a woman remade into an instrument.

artworks.title: Noire et blanche
artworks.description: Kiki's pale face resting beside a dark African mask — a charged dialogue of opposites in light and form.

artworks.title: Glass Tears (Les Larmes)
artworks.description: A model's upturned eyes with round glass beads for tears — grief staged and crystallised into surreal artifice.

name: Philip-Lorca diCorcia
tagline: Cinematic light on the seemingly candid
bio: Philip-Lorca diCorcia works in the charged gap between documentary and fiction, rigging hidden strobes on city streets and meticulously lighting domestic scenes so ordinary life looks scripted. In Hustlers he paid Los Angeles sex workers to pose, labeling each picture with their name and fee, while Heads caught anonymous Times Square passersby in sudden, theatrical illumination. His pictures made the staged and the accidental indistinguishable, redefining what a constructed photograph could be.

artworks.title: Eddie Anderson; 21 years old; Houston, Texas; $20
artworks.description: From Hustlers: a paid male sitter lit like a film still, the title pinning down name, age and fee.

artworks.title: Mario
artworks.description: A man by an open refrigerator in cold light — a banal kitchen moment staged into quiet drama.

artworks.title: Head #23
artworks.description: A Times Square passerby caught in a hidden strobe, isolated from the crowd in sudden cinematic light.

name: Ralph Eugene Meatyard
tagline: Masks and children in abandoned houses
bio: By day a Kentucky optician, Ralph Eugene Meatyard photographed his own family and friends in derelict houses, posing them with dime-store masks, dolls and blur into quietly eerie tableaux. Working far from the art world, he fused Zen, Southern gothic and Surrealism into staged scenes about time, identity and mortality. His final series, The Family Album of Lucybelle Crater, turned masked double portraits into a haunting meditation made as he was dying.

artworks.title: Romance (N.) From Ambrose Bierce #3
artworks.description: Masked children among the ruins of a peeling house — innocence staged as something uncanny.
artworks.credit: © The Estate of Ralph Eugene Meatyard

artworks.title: Untitled (Lucybelle Crater and her 40 year old husband)
artworks.description: Two figures in grotesque masks stand in a yard — the everyday double portrait pushed into ritual strangeness.
artworks.credit: © The Estate of Ralph Eugene Meatyard

name: Roger Ballen
tagline: Theatre of the absurd in chalk-marked rooms
bio: Trained as a geologist, Roger Ballen photographed in the margins of rural South Africa before retreating entirely into stark, cell-like interiors he stages himself. His square-format black-and-white pictures fill these rooms with scrawled drawings, wires, found objects, animals and human figures arranged into unsettling psychodramas. Coining the term "Ballenesque," he turned documentary roots into a wholly invented, surreal theatre poised between portrait, sculpture and drawing.

artworks.title: Dresie and Casie, Twins, Western Transvaal
artworks.description: Two drooling, identical brothers stare from a bare wall — a documentary portrait already tipping into the uncanny.

artworks.title: Eugene on the Phone
artworks.description: From Outland: a figure entangled with wires and scrawled marks in a grimy room, reality staged as nightmare.

artworks.title: Boarding House
artworks.description: A claustrophobic cell of drawings, animals and props arranged into a dense, dreamlike tableau.

name: Cindy Sherman
tagline: The self as endless invention
bio: Cindy Sherman uses her own face and body as raw material for an endless cast of invented characters, photographing herself as someone else entirely. Her breakthrough Untitled Film Stills — black-and-white pictures that look like frames from films that never existed — turned the constructed, staged photograph into a tool for dismantling the clichés of how women are pictured. She is the pivotal figure of staged, conceptual self-portraiture.

artworks.title: Untitled Film Still #21
artworks.description: The 'city girl' looking warily up between skyscrapers — a film still for a movie that never was.

artworks.title: Untitled Film Still #48 (The Hitchhiker)
artworks.description: A lone figure with a suitcase on a darkening highway — cinematic suspense built entirely by hand.

artworks.title: Untitled Film Still #56
artworks.description: A woman glancing into a mirror — identity staged, doubled and questioned.

name: Sandy Skoglund
tagline: Surreal installations built to be photographed
bio: Sandy Skoglund spends months sculpting and hand-painting elaborate installations — entire rooms overrun with luminous animals — then casts and lights live models within them to make a single tableau photograph. Her saturated, hallucinatory scenes fuse sculpture, set design and color photography into one obsessive image. By constructing the whole world in front of the lens, she pushed staged photography toward immersive, dreamlike environments.

artworks.title: Radioactive Cats
artworks.description: Dozens of neon-green cats swarm a drab gray kitchen as an elderly couple sits unmoved — domesticity invaded by the uncanny.

artworks.title: Revenge of the Goldfish
artworks.description: Bright orange fish float through a blue bedroom where sleepers lie undisturbed — a dream rendered as a built set.

artworks.title: The Cocktail Party
artworks.description: Guests and furniture entirely encrusted in orange cheese curls — social ritual turned absurd and tactile.

name: Jerry Uelsmann
tagline: Darkroom montage before Photoshop
bio: Jerry Uelsmann built seamless, dreamlike black-and-white photographs decades before digital editing, combining as many as a half-dozen negatives with up to seven enlargers in a single printing session. Trees float over water, rooms open onto skies, and hands cradle whole landscapes in images he almost always left "Untitled" so viewers could supply their own meaning. A pioneer of composite, surreal photography, he proved the darkroom could be a place of pure invention rather than mere record.

artworks.title: Untitled (floating tree over water)
artworks.description: A great tree and its roots hover above a still lake — gravity quietly suspended through darkroom montage.

artworks.title: Apocalypse II
artworks.description: A brooding composite of figure, landscape and looming cloud — premonitory imagery assembled from many negatives.

name: Francesca Woodman
tagline: Spectral self-portraits in decaying rooms
bio: In a brief, intense career cut short at twenty-two, Francesca Woodman made haunting black-and-white self-portraits in which her own body blurs, hides behind peeling wallpaper, or dissolves into the long exposure of a derelict room. Spectral, intimate and surreal, her work bridges Surrealism and contemporary staged self-portraiture — a direct ancestor of the kind of solitary, constructed picture Kyle Thompson would later make.

artworks.title: Space², Providence, Rhode Island
artworks.description: Her body pressed into a broken cabinet in an empty room — presence and disappearance in one frame.

artworks.title: House series, Providence
artworks.description: A blurred figure merging with peeling walls — the long exposure turning the self into a ghost.

artworks.title: Untitled, Rome
artworks.description: Drapery, mirror and shadow stage a fragile, dreamlike disappearance.
